passage: So you want the real story? Okay. I'm Gurleen, and last March I watched my best friend Yamini slide a folded chit out of her sock during the chemistry final. Nobody else saw. I did. For two days I couldn't eat properly. Part of me kept saying, she's your person, since class three, you don't do this to her. The other part kept seeing Farah, who studies till midnight and scored four marks less than Yamini. I didn't tell the teacher. I also didn't pretend it was fine. I waited till we were alone on the stairs and said, "I saw the chit. I'm not going to report you, but I can't act like I didn't see. Please tell Ma'am yourself." She cried, then got angry, then went quiet. When she offered me her chits for the physics paper, I said no. Did she confess? Not that week. But she stopped.

qa.q: What did Yamini take out of her sock during the chemistry final?
qa.a: Yamini slid a folded chit out of her sock during the chemistry final.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling in the two days after the exam?
qa.a: Gurleen felt torn and uneasy: loyalty to a friend since class three pulled one way, and fairness to Farah, who studied till midnight, pulled the other, so Gurleen could hardly eat.

qa.q: What did Gurleen get right in how the problem was handled?
qa.a: Gurleen spoke to Yamini privately, asked her to tell the teacher herself, and refused to join in when offered chits for the next paper.

qa.q: How might Yamini have seen that talk on the stairs?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt caught and hurt at first, which is why she cried and got angry, but she may also have felt that Gurleen was still on her side by not reporting her.

grounding: It shows a teen who knows a best friend copied, feels torn between loyalty and honesty, and privately urges the friend to come clean without joining in.

Thursday. At the bus stop Simran laughed about her ninety-two. Chaitanya kept his voice low. "I saw your phone on Monday. I'm not telling anyone, but it wasn't fair to the rest of us. You should tell Mr D'Souza before the marks go on the board." Simran snapped that he was supposed to be her friend. He said, "I am. That's why I'm saying it to you and not about you."

The next Tuesday. Simran messaged him a photo of the formula page before the retest and wrote, "Just in case." Chaitanya deleted it without opening the full image and replied, "Not doing this. Want to revise together tonight instead?" After a long pause she sent, "Fine. Library, five o'clock."

14 Nov, late

Dear diary, today was the worst Thursday of the year. Everyone knows it was me. Last week I told Sir that Karan and three others had the answers from a leaked link. I didn't want to. I sat with it for two nights, thinking about the kids who study with torches when the power goes. Then I went to the staffroom.

Today Karan said, loud enough for the whole row, "Thomas the traitor." Even Joel, who I've sat beside since Class 6, turned his chair away. I felt sick in the canteen and threw away half my roll.

But Ankita walked over and put her tray next to mine. She didn't say anything big. She just said, "You did what I didn't have the guts to do." We ate. It helped more than I can write.

I still feel like a traitor sometimes. Maybe that feeling and being right can both be true.

Thomas

I'm Noor, and I used to think being liked meant saying yes. Then came the take-home economics test in Class 11. The night before it was due, the class group lit up: "Noor send ur answers pls," "just the long ones," "don't be selfish yaar." Sarika even called and said everyone would hate me if I didn't.

I typed "okay" three times and deleted it three times. My chest felt tight. In the end I wrote, "I can't share answers, it's a graded test. But I'm free at seven. Anyone who wants to go over chapter four with me can join a call."

A few people left the group chat in protest. Someone posted an eye-roll. But at seven, Sarika joined, and two others. We worked through supply curves until nine. Sarika said, "Okay, this actually makes sense now." Not everyone forgave me. I could live with that.

"Promise you won't tell anyone," Kashish said, sitting on the low wall behind the bus stand.

"Tell what?" Maria asked.

"The English test. I wrote the poem summaries on the inside of my water bottle label."

Maria didn't answer for a moment. "Kash…"

"Everyone does something! And if Ma'am asks, just say we were revising together in the library before, okay? Then it looks like I studied."

"I'm listening, and I'm not going to go around telling people," Maria said slowly. "But I can't say I was with you in the library. I wasn't."

"So you're choosing a test over me?"

"No. I'm choosing not to lie for you. That's different." Maria shifted closer. "You're scared, I get it. What if you tell Ma'am yourself before she finds out? I'll come with you to the staffroom."

Kashish picked at the wall. "You'd come?"

"Yes. Tomorrow, first break."

Looking back at Class 9, the hardest week wasn't an exam. It was the Friday Nilesh caught me after football and said, "Arnab, I need to tell you something and you can't be weird."

He'd seen the answer key for the geography test lying on Sir's table during a free period and memorised half of it. He looked awful telling me, hands jammed in his pockets. Then came the real ask: "If anyone asks, I was with you at the ground the whole free period. Please."

I remember wanting to say yes just to make his face stop looking like that. Instead I said, "I'm glad you told me. I don't think you're a bad person. But I wasn't with you, and I won't say I was. I think you should talk to Sir before he finds out another way."

He didn't talk to me for two days. On Monday he told me he'd gone to Sir. The test was retaken by everyone.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Arnab to say he did not think Nilesh was a bad person?
qa.a: It let Nilesh feel heard and not judged, which made the refusal to be an alibi easier to accept and the push to confess easier to act on.

qa.q: What would have changed if Arnab had agreed to be the alibi?
qa.a: Arnab would have been lying to protect cheating, and Nilesh might never have gone to Sir, so the unfair result might have stood.

Wednesday, 9:40 pm

Today Rekha ma'am held up two history papers with the exact same wrong date and said, "I know some of you know who shared. Whoever it is, come and see me." Then silence, the kind where you can hear the fan.

I know it was Aman and Dev. Dev showed me the photos before the test and I said no. I felt my ears go hot the whole time she was talking.

passage:
The day I got the state essay prize, Nandini stopped waiting for me after school. I'm Dilnaz, and we had written our entries side by side in the reading room, sharing one pencil sharpener and a lot of complaints.

At first I thought she was just busy. Then I saw her looking away when my name was read in assembly, and I understood. She had wanted it as much as I did.

I felt two things at once: proud and guilty. My aunt wanted me to post the certificate everywhere. I didn't. I also didn't say "it's nothing," because it wasn't, and Nandini would have known I was lying.

I wrote her one message: "I miss walking home with you. Your essay made me rewrite my ending, you know. If you ever want to swap drafts again, I'm here." She didn't reply for a week. Then she left a new draft on my desk, no note.

qa.q: What did Nandini leave on Dilnaz's desk?
qa.a: Nandini left a new draft on Dilnaz's desk, with no note.

qa.q: What two feelings did Dilnaz have after the prize?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt proud of winning and guilty that the win had hurt Nandini, who had wanted the prize just as much.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Dilnaz not to post the certificate everywhere?
qa.a: Flaunting the win would have deepened Nandini's hurt, while staying quiet let Dilnaz reach out without rubbing it in. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nandini see the message Dilnaz sent?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt seen and credited, since Dilnaz admitted her essay shaped the ending, which could explain the draft she finally left.

grounding: It shows a teen whose win makes a friend turn cold, staying gracious, crediting the friend and reaching out once.

passage:
Saturday

Science fair results are out and I came second. Charu came first. Again. Her water-filter model was genuinely brilliant, the way she layered the charcoal and sand, and I told her so at the stall. She told me my solar dryer was "annoyingly clever." We both laughed like idiots.

Then on the bus Kunal and Rishi started on me. "You're supposed to hate her, bro. You're going soft." I almost said, "Charu? She's just lucky." The words were right there. I felt my face go hot and I hated that I cared what they thought.

I didn't say it. I said, "She's my friend and she beat me fair. Next year I'm beating her." They groaned. Whatever.

Honestly, having Charu to chase is the best part. She makes me check every wire twice. I'm going to ask her if we can test our designs together before the district round, just the two of us arguing about it.

— Yogesh

qa.q: Which model did Charu make?
qa.a: Charu made a water-filter model.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Kunal and Rishi teased Yogesh on the bus?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and annoyed, with a hot face, because their opinion mattered and the urge to deny the friendship with Charu was strong.

qa.q: Which choice worked on the bus, and why?
qa.a: Calling Charu a friend who won fairly worked, because it kept the friendship honest while still showing Yogesh wanted to beat her next time.

qa.q: How might Charu see Yogesh's plan to test their designs together?
qa.a: Charu would likely enjoy it, since she already joked warmly about the solar dryer and seems to like being pushed by a rival she respects.

grounding: It shows two fierce rivals who admire each other's work, the temptation to deny the friendship to avoid looking soft, and the choice to let the rivalry push both.
